en: The myriad spirits are all in a state of restless agitation; they take the Unsurpassed Way and interpret it through written words. Our Buddha, ever-vigilant and clear-sighted, uses these very words to illuminate the ground of the mind.
He expounds the Three Baskets and the Twelve Divisions of the Canon, encompassing the vastness of the Dharma-realm and penetrating as subtly as a mote of dust.
He declares that the Great Void resides within the human heart, such that within a single speck of dust or a single hair, there are immeasurable Buddhas.

The world. The Great Compassion of the Buddha extends throughout the great trichiliocosm; there is not a single thing that He does not deliver, and He will surely continue until all sentient beings have been saved before He rests.
How magnificent is the Dharma King! Who would have thought that there would again appear these five thousand four hundred volumes of inconceivable and immeasurable Dharma-treasures?
Since the arrival of this Sūtra in the Eastern Land, several millennia have passed, up to the present day.

Among those prevalent in the world, none can compare to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Truly, because the words of this sūtra are concise and its meaning is refined, it is the Way of returning to simplicity.

When I, a fool, have frequently read this sūtra with deep investigation, it was as if I were polishing a block of jade until it is complete, or peeling away the layers of a plantain tree until it is exhausted.
This is because when human desires are completely purified, the Heavenly Principle flows forth; once the core of the plantain has been fully peeled away, [only the truth remains].
Only then will one realize the wondrous hand [of the Buddha]. Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is indeed a great method for purifying the mind.

The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is also called the *Sūtra of Merit*. Since beginningless time, the layers upon layers of karmic debts—whether from enemies or kin, whether sin or merit—have been like a silkworm spinning its cocoon;
it entangles and binds itself, never to be liberated. This sutra is like drawing silk from that cocoon; suddenly, one attains sudden awakening.

To sever [delusions], to untangle the entanglements and remove the bonds for others, and to manifest one's own innate, natural nature—this is the great turning point that transcends the mundane and enters the sacred, whereby even enmity and kinship are resolved into equality.

When I was a child, upon reading this sutra to the passage, "Abiding thus, thus subduing the mind," I had a sudden realization. Subsequently, I read the commentaries of the ancient masters, which state: [...]* *Note: The source text appears to be truncated at this point.*
Regarding the phrase "one who is thus trained is the Way," some claim that this refers to the following words; both interpretations are without fault.
However, the Chan school maintains that the Way resides in mental realization and not in language or written characters. Thus, our Buddha preached the Dharma for forty-nine years.
Not a single word has been uttered, yet every word reveals the capacity for awakening, entering, and realization.
For one who understands well, when the path of mental activity is cut off and the way of speech is severed, it is like a person drinking water—the coldness or warmth is known by oneself alone.
One cannot weep; one cannot laugh. Only then is one a true reader of the sutras. However, this may be spoken to those who already know; it cannot yet be explained to others.

This is a general account of the Master. He attained the seal of mind in this Way through his fellow practitioner, Xie Zi. After extensively studying the various scriptures for over ten years, he gained a personal and intimate realization of the Way.
Feeling that one should not shrink from the task of benevolence, he resolved to shoulder the burden of transmission;

thus, with his mouth as a brush hanging on the wall and his hand reaching toward the void, he composed the *Easy Explanation of the Diamond Sutra* in one volume, which he has now presented for inspection.

Upon examining it, every word reveals the sublime truth and every character provides the authentic explanation. It awakens the faculty for realization and entry, like a string of *maṇi* jewels threaded together;
it truly possesses the wondrous power of "dotting the eyes" to break through the wall. Furthermore, it is like a seamless celestial robe, perfectly rounded and without a trace of a seam.
This is truly a great joy for all time, and it does not fail to be an easy-to-understand work. If one were to obtain this...

Read it thus. Those who have not yet attained realization may follow it to perceive the Way; even those who have already attained realization may use it to verify their silent comprehension and mental penetration.
When neither person nor ox is seen, the four marks will all be cast off. This is more than merely having the jewel in one's garment at hand;
it is the succession to the Buddha’s legacy. Since the lineage of the Way has its rightful place, one should naturally rejoice throughout one's life in this peerless excellence.
This has been so from antiquity to the present. Among those in the world who possess discernment, there will surely not regard these foolish words as mere empty talk. This serves as the preface.
Composed by Tang Yangyu, a descendant of Nanzong from Zhupu named Laiyunzi, during the late spring of the Jichou year of the Guangxu era.
Regarding the Inner Canon, I have never previously studied it in depth; at first, I did not know what its Way was like. It was only when I took up my pen...
While serving in the military, he served under the same command as Guan San and Xie Zi. Morning and evening they engaged in pure conversation (*qingtan*), from which he received much inspiration.
He became a man refined beyond the mundane world, whose discourse was not that of ordinary secular society.

Having associated with him for a long time, I came to know that he had thoroughly researched and mastered the Great Way of the Three Teachings, and that he had attained particularly profound realization in the sutras and treatises of the Śākya school. Only then did I suddenly realize...
Yet, that they harbor their radiance and conceal their brilliance, remaining serene and free from worldly ambition, is truly for good reason. I often say:

throughout the few decades of human life, people exhaust their spirit and deplete their wisdom and deliberation merely to expand their own bodies and households; they live in vain and die in futility, with sorrow and suffering following one after another.
To fail to contemplate liberation amidst this is truly a great pity. This is especially so for those of our kind, who furthermore dwell beyond the kalpas.
"Through successive lives, one has been buffeted by the vicissitudes of the world. Upon hearing this, I could not help but feel my heart stir with emotion.
Consequently, I took up a stone-commentary on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and instructed myself to recite, study, and investigate it, whereby I naturally obtained benefit.

Yet, when I first read it, I was utterly unable to understand it; though I questioned others about it, I still did not grasp its meaning clearly. Only after practicing it for a long time did [the meaning] from the past...
That which was previously not understood is now understood; that which was previously understood is now further advanced by one level.

Through long-term investigation and inquiry, the more one seeks, the more marvelous it becomes. As the mind-ground daily advances toward clarity and brilliance, one finally realizes the wondrousness of this sutra—its excellence being such that it cannot be fully described in words. How great is the Buddha’s compassion throughout the great trichiliocosm!
"All sentient beings, down to the most minute insects, shall be universally delivered; one must surely continue until all beings are delivered before ceasing.
Truly these words are so; they are certainly no empty speech. Yet, the Sūtra further states: "If there are sentient beings who are to be delivered by the Tathāgata..."
The Tathāgata speaks of "self," "persons," "sentient beings," and "lifespan" merely because one must see one's own nature to achieve liberation.
The sūtras spoken by the Buddha do nothing more than untie the knots and remove the bonds for the sake of others; he bestows no substantial dharma upon anyone. Thus it is said:

"The Dharma I have taught is like the parable of the raft. Now, as we gradually distance ourselves from the Buddha and it becomes difficult to encounter true spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), if we do not rely upon the sūtras...

Chinese characters. To investigate them for oneself—how could one possibly attain liberation through such means? Therefore, I have been reading the sutras until I reached the passage on the "mark of selflessness, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, and the mark of a life-span.
I realized that as long as these four marks are not eliminated, it will ultimately be difficult to make progress.
The delusive thoughts of us humans are chaotic and manifold; we must sweep away all external conditions, just as one cuts a handful of tangled threads—once severed, they are all gone at once.

Only when afflictions are severed does one possess the capacity for affinity with the Path. Furthermore, the scriptural passages stating that "one should dwell nowhere" and "one should dwell thus, thus subduing the mind," etc., contain profound meaning;
they must be carefully contemplated and savored before the essential method for purifying the mind can be perceived.
However, once practice has continued for a long time, the innate nature will spontaneously manifest, occurring as it does without being sought.

This is not something that those who are not of the inner circle can fail to recognize; however, the purport of the Sūtra is profoundly deep, and without relying on direct instruction, it is difficult to comprehend at once.
Now, for over ten years, you have refined your wisdom-mind and wisdom-nature through diligent inquiry and silent realization, reaching a state of profound mastery.

Having suddenly resolved to shoulder this great responsibility, you have employed the hand of one who knows how to "dot the eyes" [to bring a painting to life] and composed a single volume of the *Easy Explanation of the Diamond Sūtra*.
Although these words are simple and direct, they succinctly point toward the perfect, wondrous truth;

they are truly sufficient to awaken the capacity for realization in others and to serve as a bridge for future students to ascend together upon the path to enlightenment. This is indeed a great joy for all time, past and present.
May all who see or hear this cultivate and realize it together, so that one day we may gather once more at the assembly on Vulture Peak.
Excellent connection. It was solely because [Master] Zhe did not fail to take a single piece of compassionate heart as his guiding principle that this came to pass.

Having long relied upon the "other mountain" (his teachings) and deeply benefited from its "beautiful moisture," I have now briefly recounted the origins of these circumstances regarding the completion of the printing of the commentary on the sutra, to inform my fellow practitioners so that we may celebrate it together.
Respectfully preface by Liu Shaonan, a lay practitioner of Yuanjue Monastery in Zhenzhou, during the first ten days of the fourth month of the late spring in the Jichou year of the Guangxu era:
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is the fountainhead of the mind of all Buddhas and the life-force of wisdom for all sentient beings.

Therefore, its exposition of the Dharma of the mind is concise yet comprehensive and clear; it sweeps away all flowery rhetoric and uniquely proclaims true enlightenment. Indeed, since the Buddha-dharma came from the West...
From the time of the single-lineage transmission from above, there has been nothing that did not take this as the ladder and vessel for entering the Way; it is truly a treasure of the Dharma.

When the various masters of the Linji school emerged, they established Zen mechanisms, employing the striking of staffs and shouts, eschewing language, and pointing directly to the realization of one's nature.
They seemed to wish to set aside all the scriptures on high shelves; though this appeared to open a new path, it was in fact derived from *can* (investigation).

Among those who study [the teachings], there are those who do not strive to contemplate the mind, but instead merely engage in outward pursuit, thereby incurring the censure of "chewing on the description of food" or "counting another's treasures.
Thus, they are made to temporarily cease external conditions and sever their entanglements so that the true and eternal may be revealed alone;
this is specifically intended to remedy the defects of the times. This is not the fault of the scriptures, but rather the fault of those who do not properly recite and study them. Therefore...
During the Tang dynasty, there were already over eight hundred schools of commentary on this sutra.
Indeed, it is the ladder and the vessel for entering the Way, and the primary task for those who study the mind.

Yet, considering that various commentaries have appeared and disappeared, or been preserved and lost, they no longer appear together in the world. Those that remain today still number in the dozens, such as that by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.

Furthermore, the various treatises and commentaries by the great virtuous ones—whether concerning meditation or doctrine—expound the Buddha’s intent without failing to exhaustively reveal its subtle nuances;
each reaches its own excellence. However, because their language and meaning are profound and obscure, they are not easily understood by those of beginner's capacity.

Now, this sutra circulates throughout the land, with almost every household reciting and practicing it; yet, if one seeks to clarify its fundamental tenets and enter [the path] through it, [one must rely on these works].
The Way is ultimately not encountered often; is this not because the profound *prajñā* is difficult to investigate thoroughly, and furthermore, one lacks the means of guidance?
In recent times, only Master Shí Tiānjī has provided a commentary on this sutra that is most detailed;

yet it is felt to be overly circuitous and restrictive, making it difficult for others to achieve sudden enlightenment. As for myself, I have long been devoted to the recitation and study of this sutra, and in my leisure...

I have constantly sought out its essential intent and further benefited from the critical refinement of virtuous friends; thus, although my natural disposition is dull and ignorant, it seems I have gained some slight understanding.
Therefore, disregarding my own stubborn rusticity, I have annotated the entire work and titled it the *Yìjiě* (Easy Explanation).

Within it, I have frequently extended and elucidated the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*yúanyì*). Some may say that this sutra belongs to the Sudden Teaching (*dùnjiào*), yet now it is appended to [the Gradual Teaching].
Does this not contradict the judgments of the ancient schools? However, the *Lotus Sūtra* speaks of the three animals crossing the river and the three vehicles leaving the house;

the Dharma has no dual nature—it is only that the individuals differ. Those who read this sūtra, if they can attain a silent resonance with its meaning and penetrate it from all sides, [will realize this truth].
Thus, entering the perfect [teaching] directly is not something outside one's capacity. In all my commentaries, with the exception of philological glosses, everything else is my own humble insight;
I by no means pick up the "tooth-wisdom" of others to mark it as my own or to covet credit for the work.

Regarding all sutras and śāstras, I also dare not cite them extensively or draw upon a vast array of sources, lest people easily become weary and their spiritual faculties be stifled. Those who aspire to explore the ultimate source [should understand this].
Perhaps this may serve as an aid like that of an aged horse. However, my learning and experience are meager and shallow;
yet, speaking of the scriptures with all my heart, I cannot avoid the reproach of speaking recklessly. Should those of superior intelligence deign to instruct me, it would be most fortunate.
Preface by the Layman from Piling, Xie Chengmu, alias Guansan, on the full moon of the third lunar month in the year of Jichou,
the fifteenth year of the Guangxu era.
First, the ancient masters have classified this sutra as the Sudden Teaching (*dun jiao*), because it points directly to Bodhi without any further elaboration or branches.
Furthermore, because one enters through a single gate without being equipped with all the various practices, it is specifically termed "Sudden" rather than "Complete" (*yuan*).
I, however, maintain that this sutra is both Sudden and Complete. Why is this? Although the sutra initially clarifies emptiness (*śūnyatā*), [it subsequently reveals the nature of phenomena].

Furthermore, it is said that regarding the Dharma, one does not speak of characteristics of annihilation or extinction. Now, where annihilation and non-existence do not persist, this is precisely the Middle Way.
The "Middle" (madhyama) carries the meaning of "perfect" (pariniṣpanna). It is further stated: "The *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* attained by the Tathāgata..."
Within this, there is neither reality nor emptiness. Where there is neither reality nor emptiness, existence and non-existence cannot be established.

When existence and non-existence are not established, it is neither existent nor non-existent. Being neither existent nor non-existent, it encompasses both existence and non-existence. Thus, existence and non-existence are fully integrated.

This is the simultaneous illumination of both and the simultaneous extinction of both; it even transcends both "is" and "is not," being both "is" and "is not. It reveals the Real by opening the Provisional, and is the Provisional within the Real;
it establishes the Provisional for the sake of the Real, and is the Real within the Provisional. This is the Perfect [Teaching] contained within the Sudden.
As for the Buddha’s teaching that "the foremost *pāramitā* is not the foremost *pāramitā*;

it is called the foremost *pāramitā*," there are many such instances of the threefold formula in the sūtras. If one extends this principle further, then even the threefold formula encompasses the meaning of the fourfold formula;
is this not the simultaneous presence of the Sudden and the Perfect? The fourfold formula refers to existence... [and so forth].
The phrase "the phrase of non-phrase," "the phrase of neither existence nor non-existence," and "the phrase of both existence and non-existence" allow for an immediate entry through a single gate;
yet, as they do not fully encompass all dharmas, they may merely be called "inclusive and perfect" (*jiānyuán*), but cannot be called "purely perfect" (*chúnyuán*).

However, according to the four teachings of the Tiantai school, it is said that the *Prajñā* [teaching] incorporates the Shared (*tōng*) and Distinct (*bié*) while clarifying the Perfect (*yuán*); thus, the doctrine of "inclusive perfection" is established.
This is not false. In general, the Dharma has no fixed direction; its depth or shallowness depends on the person. When a wise person sees it, they call it wisdom;
when a benevolent person sees it, they call it benevolence. This lies solely in the individual’s own realization (the Tiantai school’s four teachings refer to the *zang*, *tong*, *bie*, and *yuan*).
One should cultivate contemplation in accordance with the teaching. The contemplative methods of this sutra are complete and its stages are orderly.

As it was previously stated: "All that has marks is entirely illusory; if one sees that all marks are non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata. This is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).
"Knowing that all things are empty, for dharmas are also like illusions. It continues: "Do not harbor this thought:
'The Tathāgata has attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of marks of perfection.
This is the contemplation of the provisional (parikalpita), knowing that all names and characteristics arise from conditions. It further states: "That which the Tathāgata has attained..."
Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Within this, there is neither reality nor emptiness; this is precisely the Middle Way.
It is because one thoroughly understands that form is itself emptiness and emptiness is itself form, and that the one is all and all is one.
If one wishes to practice this method of contemplation, one can enter the provisional from emptiness and clarify the middle through the provisional.
Within the past, present, and future, the three minds are difficult to find; the four marks of self, person, sentient being, and life-span are all completely dissolved.
Mind seals mind, and every thought is non-thought; thus, one attains the definitive meaning of the Middle Way. This is the process of entering the profound from the shallow, gradually...
To "tread the Middle Way" means that within the sudden [enlightenment] there is a gradual process.
The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma is entered through faith; thus it is said, "Faith is the source of the Way and the mother of merit. Faith is able to nurture all roots of goodness.
This is as explained in the sutras regarding the comparison of the magnitude of merits, as well as the worlds as numerous as motes of dust.
Such matters are indeed true and not deceptive. One must not, because they have not personally heard or seen them, dismiss them as mere hyperbolic rhetoric.
Consider this: how could the sincere words of the Golden Mouth (the Buddha) contain any falsehood?

Even if you cannot yet fully penetrate this principle at once, you must believe it with earnest conviction and without doubt. There will surely come a day when all confusion will dissolve like ice melting; when that time arrives...
Only upon reaching this stage does one finally realize that the Buddha’s words are not deceptive. May all virtuous friends take this to heart and each cultivate deep faith.

Ordinary beings fear emptiness and cling to existence; those of the Two Vehicles loathe existence and grasp at emptiness. To fear emptiness and cling to existence is called the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*);

to loathe existence and grasp at emptiness is called the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). These are collectively termed inverted views (*viparyāsa-dṛṣṭi*), whether one clings to existence or clings to emptiness.
Both [extremes] constitute a sickness. This sutra is intended to instruct ordinary beings of sharp faculties;

therefore, it first refutes their attachment to signs (*nimitta*) and then sequentially compares merits to demonstrate that while conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) rewards of merit are ultimately inferior to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), giving while detached from signs far surpasses giving while attached to signs.
Furthermore, fearing that practitioners might abandon existence for emptiness, it again exhorts them with:

Not falling into either extreme, one directly transcends to the Unsurpassed. For if one remains bound by the views of annihilationism or eternalism, one ultimately becomes a mere worldling or non-Buddhist;

yet, by departing from appearances, one suddenly realizes the unborn. Which path should one follow? What is gained and what is lost? The principle is naturally easy to understand. How fortunate we are to have heard this wondrous Dharma;
how can we fail to exert ourselves in cultivation so as not to辜负 (waste) the Buddha’s compassionate and repeated exhortations?
Clear Instruction:
In reading the sutras, one must first clarify their essential tenets (*zong*). For every sutra has its own specific tenet;
if the tenet is not clarified, one will wander aimlessly without a point of return. Thus, this sutra takes non-abiding as its tenet. It is sufficient simply to realize non-abiding.
If one grasps this essential meaning, one has already attained the core of the matter; all other extensive or concise expositions are merely its secondary ramifications.

Furthermore, regarding the Dharma taught by the Buddha, it mostly revolves around the most profound and subtle points, turning in a perfect cycle like a ring, such that no beginning or end can be discerned.
Those who read the scriptures often encounter points of circularity and reciprocity and remain utterly bewildered, lacking any basis for understanding.
Their own eyes are not clear, yet they go so far as to label others "intentionally manipulative"—a case of what is called "right words appearing to be contrary.

They do not realize that the essential mystery of the Unsurpassed Great Way lies precisely in these points of circularity. If one does not speak in this manner, the principle will ultimately remain uncomprehended.

It is not yet perfectly clear and bright. If the fundamental principle is clarified, then even at places where the terrain twists and layers upon itself—where there may be myriad mountains and ten thousand ravines—one will naturally be able to comprehend them and will not be confused by them.
In the study of the scriptures, clarifying the mind is paramount; in clarifying the mind, understanding the meaning is primary.

As for the mere recitation of the scriptural texts without seeking understanding or awakening, it can only serve to assist the deceased and eliminate their transgressions, thereby producing mundane merit alone.
If one awakens to the luminous mind of the Dharma, one will immediately transcend the three realms and forever eliminate future existence.

Furthermore, all karmic enemies and kin from throughout the kalpas will be completely delivered and liberated. Is this not truly magnificent? Thus, if one wishes to clarify the ground of the mind, it is essential that the exposition of its meaning precede it;
by proceeding from words to the wordless, and from non-awakening to perfect awakening, such is the natural principle.

However, those whose innate capacities (*gotra*) are profound and who attain awakening upon hearing [the Dharma] once—realizing a thousand points at a time—are not included in this category. Yet, among the common people, few are able to do so.
Reading the sutras is not comparable to reading other books; in the case of other texts, one may read through them once and have a rough grasp of their general outline.
In general, you need not read further. As for the study and recitation of Mahāyāna sūtras, unless one is a sage, it is impossible to understand them merely by glancing over them.
One must contemplate them with a meticulous mind and engage in silent, internal inquiry; only then will their meaning emerge.
At first, one clarifies the teachings through commentaries; subsequently, one no longer requires them, but instead contemplates with single-minded depth.
After a long time, the practice will manifest of itself. As it is said, "If the mind is restrained in one place, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished.

Once one has reached that sudden, expansive realization, one finally knows that the wondrous meanings herein are inexhaustible—truly like drinking water, where its coldness or warmth is known by oneself.
One knows it, yet cannot express it to others; this is something that can only bring personal delight and is unfit to be presented as a gift to another.

Once you have attained a single scripture and achieved thorough awakening, then when you subsequently recite other scriptures, they will naturally be resolved with effortless ease, like a blade meeting the edge of a whetstone.
The explanation of Confucian texts must possess a fixed principle that cannot be altered; the Buddhist scriptures, however, are not so.
One must neither cling to them nor contradict them; this is why they are difficult. Thus, an ancient worthy said: "To rely on [the text] while also explaining its meaning."
"To be at odds with the Buddhas of the three periods of time. It is further said: "To deviate from a single word of the sūtra is to speak like a demon.

Readers, if you can find a point of entry while remaining neither stuck nor turning your back [on the teaching], and recognize that the eyebrows are horizontal and the nose is straight, only then may you read this sūtra.
The purport of this sutra is profoundly deep; it is difficult to comprehend at first glance.

If a commentator were to further employ abstruse and archaic language, the meaning would still not be clearly understood, which would be unsuitable for beginners. Therefore, this present commentary follows a generally simple and straightforward approach.

Readers may grasp its essential meaning while disregarding the literal phrasing. Moreover, since one reads a sutra solely to seek verification of the truth, what leisure is there for [elaborate commentary]?

Seeking extensively on all sides, one eventually reaches a state of sudden, liberating realization where both subject and object are forgotten. It is like suddenly beholding the morning star in the middle of a snowy night;

only then does one realize that exhausting all fundamental discernments is like placing a single hair in the vast void, and exhausting all worldly mechanisms is like casting a single drop into a great abyss.
Even if pearls and jade were to fill one’s presence, they would mean nothing to oneself.
Furthermore, at such a time, even the sutras are not required; how could there be any commentaries? They are merely like "door-knocking bricks," which one must inevitably employ for a time.
In the sūtras, the comparison of merits and the discourse on contemplating the Buddha by grasping at signs are examined with repeated scrutiny, without wearying of their detail.
Some say that because the teaching proceeds from the shallow to the profound, they appear redundant; others say it is for the sake of those who have read or heard [the teachings].

The Buddha therefore reiterates and explains them. I privately believe this is not the case. If it is claimed that [the teachings] proceed from the shallow to the profound, then upon careful examination of the essential purports of the preceding and succeeding scriptures, there is no significant difference in their repetitive passages; how then can one speak of "shallow" and "profound"?

If it is claimed that [the repetitions] are due to people listening again after having already heard [the teaching], then when the Buddha preached the Tripiṭaka scriptures, were there not indeed those who continued to listen?
How could it be that [this teaching] was not explained three times over, yet exists only in this single sutra? Such a principle is absolutely impossible.
Truly, in order to expound this rare and difficult-to-believe Dharma, the Buddha observed the minds of the assembly with his eye of wisdom;
he knew full well that unless it were explained three or five times, they would be unable to believe it with complete clarity and without doubt. Therefore, he did not weary of [repeating it].

The prolixity of the discourse is for the sake of great compassion. Furthermore, the Buddha’s teachings frequently take Subhūti as his witness to clarify that there is no divergence, because the nature of phenomena is thus.
The sutras proclaim that the merit of recitation far surpasses that of bestowing precious gifts.
This is because receiving and upholding [the teachings] with faith constitutes a cause and condition for manifold roots of goodness and merit.

Furthermore, if one is unable to realize the meaning of the sutras all at once, provided one can maintain the recitation without slackening, the meaning will gradually become clear until one is capable of personal realization. However, one must not expect immediate results; until such time as...
After one has attained awakening and clarity, although the text of this sutra may appear simple and plain, its meaning remains inexhaustible. The more one seeks it, the deeper it becomes;
the more one probes it, the more wondrous it proves. Even if one were to savor and contemplate it for a lifetime, there would never be an end.
This is why this sutra is so extraordinary, and why the merit of its recitation is so preeminent. Furthermore, when reciting the sutra, one must purify oneself and eliminate [all defilements].
Dust and delusion aside, maintain single-minded concentration so that every word is distinct; this is the correct method.

It is not necessary to seek out a secluded room, but one must certainly set up an image. Recite whenever you have leisure; do not wait for a later time. You must know that the Buddha resides within your own heart.
It does not consist in outward adornment of appearance.

The Great Way of the Three Teachings follows divergent paths yet returns to the same destination; in truth, there is no duality between them. As the Sūtra says, "Emptiness eliminates the four marks," which corresponds to the "four abandonments" of the Sage.
"Non-explanation" is the Sage’s "wordlessness. The Five Precepts are the Five Constant Virtues. The Three...
The "poisons" are precisely the Three Refuges; the universal salvation of self and others is precisely the "illumination and renewal" (*mingxin*) of the *Great Learning*;

and the impartial benefit derived from the gift of the Dharma is precisely the "establishment and nourishment" (*weiyu*) of the *Doctrine of the Mean*. In these various ways they correspond; words are insufficient to fully describe them.

One might wonder whether Buddhism differs [from Confucianism], yet as for the subtle and profound essence of the wondrous Way—matters of which the sages rarely spoke—the Buddha has explained them in detail.

We were born in the age of decline. Had it not been for the scriptures of Śākyamuni, how could we have come to understand such principles as "refining the single-mindedness" and "holding fast to the Mean," "returning to benevolence," and "abiding in the world and nourishing all things," as well as the purport of the "One Thread" and "wordlessness"?
This is truly what东坡 (Dongpo) meant when he said that one only comes to know Confucianism after studying Buddhism. It is indeed so.
This sutra is like a celestial robe without seams; originally, there were no discernible sections to be found.

It was only when the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu first divided it into twenty-seven points of doubt that it became so structured. For instance, regarding the gift of jewels, the merit of upholding and expounding [this sutra] surpasses it;
because Subhūti repeatedly gave rise to doubts, the Buddha sequentially provided explanations for him, desiring to cause his doubts to be severed and faith to arise.

Therefore, Prajñāpāramitā is called the Mother of the Buddhas.
Subhūti, that which is called the Buddha-dharma is not, in fact, the Buddha-dharma.
Fearing that upon hearing this sutra’s sublime Dharma, they might again give rise to attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), the Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying:

"That which is called the Buddha-dharma of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment is the cause for awakening through each encounter with forms and sounds; it is not something that exists as a substantial entity."
The certainty of death may indeed be called the Buddha-dharma.
Chapter Nine: The Section on One Aspect and Aspectlessness. Regarding "one aspect": it is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
Although it is said that all phenomena possess a true reality, upon ultimate investigation, they lack any fixed characteristic. It is therefore clear that one ought not to grasp or cling to them.
Subhūti, what do you think? Does a srotāpanna (stream-enterer) have this thought: "I have attained the fruit of srotāpanna"? [Note:

*Srotāpanna* is pronounced *huàn* hereafter. *Srotāpanna* translates in Chinese as "entering the stream," meaning that this person has already severed the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*) and has entered the stream of the noble ones (*ārya*).
"Delusions of views" refers to the mental calculations that arise when perceiving phenomena.
This is a deliberation. The Buddha, wishing to show people the principle of realizing the Way by departing from signs, called out to Subhūti and asked him:
"In your opinion, what do you think? Among the Śrāvaka vehicle, there are four fruits; the first fruit is named Srotāpanna.
One who realizes this fruit thinks in their mind: "I have now attained the stage of Srotāpanna."
"Is it so? Śrāvakas belong to the Two Vehicles; they are so called because they realize the fruit by hearing the sound of the Dharma being preached.
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Subhūti was one who had already traversed this path;
therefore, upon hearing the Buddha's question, he knew that one who realizes such a fruit must certainly not harbor even a single thought of attaining a fruit.
Therefore, he answered with "No. Why is this?
The name *srotāpanna* means "one who has entered the stream," yet there is nothing entered.
The reason a *srotāpanna* does not harbor a mind that seeks to attain a fruit is because, in truth, a *srotāpanna* merely possesses the entry into the stream.
It is called "Stream-enterer," yet it lacks the mark of entering a stream.
Not entering into form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas—this is called a Srotāpanna.

Since a Srotāpanna does not become attached to the marks of attaining a fruit, they have no defiled attachment whatsoever toward the objects of the six sense-fields; therefore, they are called a Srotāpanna.
“Srotāpanna. “Subhūti, what do you think? Does a Sakṛdāgāmin have the thought: ‘I have attained the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin’?
Here, the Buddha enumerates the four fruits of spiritual attainment and questions him regarding them. *Sakṛdāgāmin* translates in the vernacular as “Once-returner.”
This person has already severed six grades of the nine grades of afflictions of thought (*vitarka*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Since they must still undergo one more birth in the desire realm, they are called "Once-returners" (*sakṛdāgāmin*). "Afflictions of thought" refers to the arising of the mind at every moment of contact.
The Buddha addressed Subhūti and questioned him again, saying: "In the Śrāvaka vehicle, the second fruit is named Sakṛdāgāmin. One who realizes this fruit..."
He wonders to himself, "Have I now attained the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin?
Subhūti replies, "No, World-Honored One. Subhūti answers with "No" because even a person who has attained the first fruit does not harbor the thought that they have attained a fruit;
how much less so for those who have attained higher stages? Therefore, he likewise answers with "No."
Why is this? One who is called a *sakṛdāgāmin* (once-returner) is in reality without coming or going; thus is he named a *sakṛdāgāmin*.
As for why it is said that a *sakṛdāgāmin* does not harbor the thought of attaining a fruit:
although a *sakṛdāgāmin* possesses the designation of "coming and going," his mind is devoid of the marks of coming and going. For this reason, he is named a *sakṛdāgāmin*.
[The Buddha] said, "Subhūti, what do you think? Does an Anāgāmin (one who does not return) have the thought: 'I have attained the fruit of an Anāgāmin'? [Anāgāmin;
*āna* means "not," *ro* (pronounced *la* hereafter) means "to come. Anāgāmin is translated into Chinese as "One Who Does Not Return. Such a person, regarding the desire realm...
Having completely severed the afflictions of the nine grades of thought, one no longer returns to take birth in the desire realm;
therefore, it is called "Non-returner" (Anāgāmin). The Buddha again addressed Subhūti and questioned him, saying: "Among those of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the third fruit is named Anāgāmin.
When one realizes this fruit, does his mind think, 'I have now attained the fruit of Anāgāmin'?"
Subhūti said, "No, World-Honored One. Subhūti answered with "No" because even an *anāgāmin* does not maintain the thought of attaining the fruit.
Why is this? Anāgāmin is named "one who does not come," yet in reality there is no such thing as "not coming";
thus he is called Anāgāmin. As for why it is said that an Anāgāmin does not harbor the thought of attaining a fruit:
although his name is "one who does not come," his mind is likewise free from the mark of "not coming. Therefore, he is named Anāgāmin.
Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think? Does an Arhat have such a thought as, "I have attained the path of Arhatship"?
An Arhat—whose name in the language of China means "One Beyond Training"—has completely severed and exhausted all afflictions within the three realms.
Ultimate truth is not something that can be learned; therefore, it is called "no-more-learning" (aśaikṣa).
Furthermore, because an Arhat is about to enter the Buddha-vehicle, he speaks of the Path rather than the Fruit. The Buddha then addressed Subhūti and questioned him, saying:
The four fruits of the Śrāvaka vehicle are called Arhatship. Does one who has realized these fruits think, "I have now attained the path of an Arhat"?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. This is because Subhūti, as an Arhat, has completely exhausted all afflictions.
How could one still maintain the thought of attaining the Way? Therefore, he answered with "No. Why is this?
Truly, there is no dharma named Arhat. As for why it is said that an Arhat does not maintain the thought of attaining the Way:
it is because an Arhat has indeed attained the dharma of signlessness (*animitta*). However, truly...
"One who has no thought of attaining the Dharma is called an Arhat.
"World-Honored One, if an Arhat were to think, 'I have attained the path of Arhatship,' he would then be attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "If an Arhat’s mind were to form such a thought..."
It means that if one has already attained the right path of Arhatship, then one's mind is already attached to signs (*nimitta*).
Since one is attached to the sign of having attained the Way, one is likewise attached to the four signs such as self (*ātman*) and person (*pudgala*). How, then, can one be called an Arhat?

“World-Honored One, the Buddha has declared that I have attained the *araṇā-samādhi* (the samādhi of non-contention), that I am the foremost among men, and that I am the foremost *arhat* free from desire.
*Samādhi*—in the language of China, it is called *zhèngshòu* (right reception), which refers to the wondrous principle.
Subhūti further corroborated this with what he himself had attained; thus, addressing the World-Honored One, he said: “The Buddha sees me and...”
All things are without contention, yet I am called one who has already attained the Samādhi of Non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*).
Among men, I am the foremost and most venerable; I am an Arhat of the highest rank, capable of liberation from the five desires.
Indeed, were it not for the departure from desire and non-contention, one could not advance upon the Path.

I do not harbor such a thought: "I am an Arhat free from desire. Although the Buddha has indeed designated me as an Arhat free from desire, I have never actually entertained the thought, "I am an Arhat free from desire."
World-Honored One, if I were to have the thought, "I have attained the path of an Arhat," then the World-Honored One would not say that Subhūti is one who delights in the practice of araṇā.
(The character for *xing* [practice] is pronounced *hen*. *Araṇā* translates into Chinese as "without contention.")

Subhūti again addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "World-Honored One, if I had ever entertained such a thought as 'I have attained the path of an Arhat,' then the World-Honored One would not have said of me, Subhūti, that I am one who delights in the practice of non-contention."
Because Subhūti has, in reality, nothing to practice, he is called "Subhūti who delights in the practice of araṇā (the state of non-conflict).
This is a practice of non-practice, according to the literal meaning of the word. "Non-practice" means practicing that which is non-existent.
As for why the Buddha praises Subhūti as having attained the samādhi of non-conflict: although Subhūti possesses cultivation and realization, [he remains free from the conflict of conceptualization].
This is simply practicing non-action. Therefore, the Buddha said that I am one who delights in the practice of non-contention;
yet, in truth, no mind of delight exists within me.
Section Ten: Adorning the Pure Land. The Dharma takes non-attainment as attainment; the mind takes non-abiding as abiding.
It is pure and spontaneous, without attachment to signs or grasping at existence. This constitutes the adorning of one’s own mind as the Pure Land.
This is not like the act of adorning [a shrine] by setting up images and making offerings.
The Buddha asked Subhūti, "What do you think? Desiring to show people his own past deeds so as to cause them to have firm faith, he said to Subhūti: "In your mind, what do you think of this?"
"When the Tathāgata was formerly with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, did he obtain anything regarding the Dharma? Here, "Tathāgata" refers to the Buddha himself.
Dīpaṃkara was the teacher of Śākyamuni. This means: "When I was formerly in the presence of my original teacher."
"Upon hearing the Dharma, I attained realization instantaneously. At that time, did my original teacher truly bestow a secret dharma upon me, such that I actually obtained something?
No, World-Honored One. Subhūti, although there is the name 'attaining the Dharma' regarding the mutual transmission from Buddha to Buddha, in reality..."

All must cultivate for themselves and deliver themselves; there is no secret dharma to bestow upon others. Without relying on cultivation and practice, one cannot attain realization of the fruit. Therefore, he answered with "No."
When the Tathāgata was with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, he truly attained nothing regarding the Dharma.
Although it is said that the Buddha formerly, while at the place of his original teacher, attained the Dharma, in reality, he attained only non-attainment. ○.
Subhūti, what do you think? Does a bodhisattva adorn buddha-fields? (The word "tǔ" [field] should be pronounced as "dù"; this is merely a difference in dialect between the East and the West.

The Buddha further feared that people would not seek to realize their own nature, but would instead focus exclusively on adorning fields through the construction of monasteries, the casting of statues, and various other decorations; therefore, he called out to Subhūti and questioned him, saying: "What is your thought?"
"What do you think? Have the bodhisattvas ever adorned buddha-fields with external marks as their adornment?
"No, World-Honored One. Subhūti [concluded] that the bodhisattvas certainly do not adorn [buddha-fields] with external marks.
In order to adorn the Buddha-field of one’s own mind, he answered with "no. Why?
Because that which is called "adorned Buddha-field" is not an adornment; it is merely named an adornment.
Now, as for what I call a bodhisattva who does not engage in the adornment of external forms—why is this so? It is because that which adorns the Buddha-field...
There is no trace of adornment; rather, each person purifies their own mind, and this is what is called "adornment.
Therefore, Subhūti, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to such a pure mind. The Buddha said:
Because the meaning of the adornment expressed by Subhūti deeply accords with its essential intent, he addresses him again, saying:
"It should be known that all bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas ought to give rise to a pure mind through such dharmas as have been described.
As for a 'pure mind,' it means that the mind does not give rise to even a single thread [of conceptualization]."
There is not the slightest trace of discursive thought. The word "arising" (sheng) is particularly essential and subtle.

The Buddha feared that practitioners might seek only mental purity, thereby remaining perpetually submerged in emptiness and clinging to stillness, becoming like withered wood or extinguished ashes; this would result in falling into partiality and desiccation rather than the Middle Way.
Therefore, he specifically spoke of "arousing a pure mind," whereby one immediately perceives a state of vibrant, lively activity.
One should not give rise to the mind by dwelling on forms; one should not give rise to the mind by dwelling on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas.

It is said that the mind of a bodhisattva should neither fall into emptiness nor cling to phenomena. Although it is called "giving rise to the mind," it should not have any attachment to the six sense objects.

"One should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere. This means that not only should one not give rise to the mind within the realm of sensory objects, but one should likewise remain free from any attachment toward all circumstances and conditions. This is the sublime method for giving rise to the mind through non-dwelling.
In our Buddha's teaching of people, there is no instruction more subtle than this; among the wondrous precepts for transmitting the mind throughout the ages, none surpass it.
In this regard, one may say that the essential words are free from prolixity; it was fitting that the Sixth Patriarch attained awakening upon hearing these words once.
Should we not exert ourselves toward this end?
Subhūti, suppose there were a person whose body was as large as Sumeru, the King of Mountains. What do you think? Would that body be great?
Sumeru rises high above the heavens and separates the four continents; its greatness is peerless, and thus it is called the King of Mountains.
The Buddha, wishing for people to perceive the greatness of the Dharma-body for themselves, employed these words to question Subhūti.
Dhīti said: "Suppose there were a person whose physical body was as vast as Sumeru, the king of mountains.
What do you think of this? Would that person's body also have been great?"
Subhūti said, “It is exceedingly great, World-Honored One. Why is this? The Buddha has taught that what is not a body is called the ‘Great Body.
Subhūti, understanding the Buddha’s intention, spoke thus: “If one were to judge by means of the physical body (*rūpakāya*), then a body like Mount Sumeru could indeed be called exceedingly great.
However, as for what is truly meant by ‘great,’ why is it so? It is simply because of the [Dharma-]body.”
This refers only to the physical body. As for what the Buddha calls the *dharmakāya*, it is as vast as empty space;
it is neither with form nor without form, and it is not the body of a physical form. Therefore, it is said to be "non-body. This may indeed be called the "Great Body";
how could it be compared to the mere, limited physical body?
Chapter Eleven: The Superiority of Unconditioned Merit. This means that although the practice of giving with the seven treasures may indeed be very extensive, it merely yields worldly, mundane merit;
such merit is finite. However, if one upholds this sutra to transform and guide others, one will ultimately attain the Way.
One will eternally enjoy non-action and true bliss; such bliss becomes ever more excellent.
Subhūti, suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River. What do you think?
Would the sands of all those Ganges Rivers be numerous? The Buddha further reiterated the merit obtained from upholding and expounding [this teaching].
Because this surpasses the gift of jewels, he calls out to Subhūti and interrogates him, saying:
"Suppose one were to take all the grains of sand in the Ganges River, and for each grain of sand, create another Ganges River. What do you think?
Would the number of sands in these Ganges Rivers created from those original sands be great? This is an extreme way of expressing its immeasurability. The Ganges is [a river] in the Western Regions.
The name of the river is [Ganges]. It is forty *li* in circumference, and its sands are exceedingly fine. The Buddha frequently preached the Dharma here;
therefore, whenever he wished to speak of something being numerous, he would immediately take the river sands as a metaphor. "Ning" means "formerly."
Subhūti said, "Very many, World-Honored One. Subhūti answered with the phrase "very many" because the number of grains of sand in the Ganges is beyond calculation.
Even the Ganges Rivers alone are already incalculably many; how much more so their sands?
To say that even the number of Ganges Rivers, calculated by the sands of a single river, is already incalculable—how could one possibly calculate the number of sands from all those rivers?

"Subhūti, I now tell you this in truth: if there were a good man or a good woman who, with the seven treasures, filled as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers and gave them as a gift, would they gain much merit?
Subhūti, because the Buddha knew that the number of sands in all those Ganges Rivers was beyond calculation, he addressed him by name.

He said: "I now tell you with words of truth: suppose there were faithful men and women here who were to fill as many great trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in the aforementioned number of rivers with the seven treasures and offer them as a gift;
would the merit they obtain not be great? In the eighth section, it was previously stated that [this refers to] the great trichiliocosm.
The merit of giving away treasures filling the worlds does not equal the merit of upholding and reciting [this teaching].

Now, to further speak of the giving of treasures filling as many great trichiliocosms as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, their abundance is even more difficult to measure, and the merit obtained is likewise inexhaustible.
The Buddha repeatedly employs metaphors to most clearly demonstrate the superiority of upholding and reciting [this teaching].
Subhūti said, "Very much, World-Honored One. Subhūti replied with "very much" because if one were to bestow such vast treasures as a gift, how could the merit obtained possibly have a limit?
Therefore, he answered that it was exceedingly great.

The Buddha told Subhūti: "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, from within this sutra, were to even receive and uphold as little as a four-line verse and explain it to others, the merit of this would surpass the former merit.
The merit obtained by giving gifts of jewels does not ultimately equal the excellence of upholding and explaining [this teaching]. Therefore, he told Subhūti: 'If there is a son of good..."
Whether it be a man or a woman who receives and upholds the chapters and verses of this sutra— even if they uphold only as little as a four-line stanza—
and furthermore explains it to others so that they may believe and accept it, the merit obtained by such a person far surpasses the merit of the previous gift of jewels.
Since the excellence of upholding and explaining it is such as this, why would people not strive for it?
Practice this. Chapter Twelve:

Honoring the True Teaching. It is said that wherever this sutra is upheld and expounded, from the devas and humans down to the asuras, all shall provide protection and guardianship; for they too know how to honor the true teaching.
Furthermore, Subhūti, wherever this sutra is spoken, even as little as a single four-line verse, this—following from the preceding chapter—declares the excellence of upholding and expounding it;
since one not only obtains immeasurable merit, he addresses Subhūti once again.

If a person explains the chapters and verses of this sutra according to their inclination—even if it be as few as four lines—one should know that this place should be honored by all the world, including devas, humans, and asuras, just like a stupa or temple.
(The word "gongyang" [供養] is pronounced with a departing tone. There are four kinds of asuras: first, those belonging to the realm of devas who are able to...
Śakra contended for parity with them. One belongs to the realm of humans, one to the realm of hungry ghosts, and one to the realm of animals.
That place where the Buddha’s śarīra is enshrined is called a *stūpa*; that place where the Buddha’s image is venerated is called a temple (*miao*).
Among all the worlds—whether devas, humans, or asuras—in any place where those who uphold and recite this sutra reside, [all beings]...
One should honor and make offerings to them as if serving the stūpas and shrines of the Buddha.
This is because that which they offer is this unsurpassed and rare Dharma, which is difficult to see and difficult to encounter; thus, having suddenly met with it, one gives rise to reverence.
How much more so for a person who is able to fully receive, uphold, read, and recite it—where "reading" refers to following the text and "reciting" refers to memorizing the text.

If even devas and humans show such profound respect for someone who merely speaks along with the chapters and phrases of the sutra, what need is there to mention the degree of veneration shown to one who can uphold and recite the entire sutra? How much greater still shall their honor be?
Subhūti, you should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme and rare Dharma.
Since this person is able to uphold and recite the entire sutra, they will certainly be able to investigate its essential meaning and may naturally enter the Path by means of it.
Therefore, the Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying: "You should know that this person who upholds the sutra does so because they have received and accepted this sutra with faith."
For this reason, one will surely be able to accomplish that most honored and supreme, foremost, and rare Dharma in the world;
thus, one's efforts shall not be in vain. Is this not truly magnificent?
"Wherever this sutra is located, there is a Buddha, as well as his honored disciples.
This means that wherever this sutra resides, although a Buddha may not be present, it is as if a Buddha were there;
and whoever upholds and recites this sutra is an honored great disciple worthy of veneration. To what extent is he to be honored?
Indeed, the excellence of this sutra is truly not slight; those who see or hear it should not fail to reverently believe, accept, and uphold it, aspiring thereby toward realization.
Chapter Thirteen: Receiving and Maintaining According to the Dharma. This section speaks of the excellence of this sutra;

having heard it, one will naturally come to revere, believe in, and maintain it. However, if one maintains it without knowing the method for generating the mind in this way, one cannot avoid entering onto a deviant path.
Therefore, it is said: "Receiving and maintaining according to the Dharma."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, what should this sutra be named? How should we uphold it?

At that moment, having heard the Buddha speak of the supreme excellence of this sutra, Subhūti was unable to contain his joy and addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, by what name should this sutra be called? Having heard this sutra, how shall we receive and maintain it?"
"You yourself should certainly believe, accept, and uphold it. But as for the method of upholding it, I do not yet know how that is to be done.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "The name of this sutra is the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. By this name..."

"You should uphold this. Because the Buddha had provided Subhūti with the essential points regarding the name of the sutra and the method for its reception and maintenance, he told him: "The name of this sutra is the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*."
This analogy shows that if one practices with a mind of firm resolve, wisdom will arise spontaneously.
Relying upon this wisdom, one proceeds directly to the other shore of Nirvana.
The reason for bestowing this name is to cause you all to reflect upon its meaning and uphold it accordingly; if you do so, you will likely attain the goal.
Why is this so? Subhūti, that which the Buddha calls the *prajñāpāramitā* is not, in fact, the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Among the sūtras spoken by the Buddha, there are those whose traces do not fall into substantiality; these are the essential and subtle points of the mind-dharma.

As for the method of upholding [the teaching] as explained above, it is because one fears that if people become attached to signs and give rise to grasping, it will no longer be the Middle Way or the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
He suddenly broke off and said, "What is the method for you all to uphold that I have taught? Subhūti, you should know this:
the purport of the Buddha’s teaching on the Prajñāpāramitā is simply that when it is realized within the mind, that itself is it."
This does not mean that one should constantly maintain the view of the *prajñāpāramitā* within one's breast.
This point must be most carefully distinguished; for as the saying goes, "a hair’s breadth of difference leads to worlds apart."

"Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata preached any dharma? The Buddha called upon Subhūti and questioned him in this way because he wished to extensively dispel the notion of signs (*nimitta*). He asked: "In your mind, what do you think?
Since the Tathāgata has constantly preached the Dharma for you all, is there indeed any real dharma that has been given to others?"
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has nothing to speak.

Having heard the Buddha’s words, Subhūti understood with certainty that for one who preaches the Dharma, there is the meaning of having no dharma whatsoever to speak; therefore, he immediately addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One."
Although the Tathāgata speaks of the Dharma, in reality, he says nothing at all.
Subhūti, what do you think? Are all the atoms contained within a trichiliocosm many?
This is because the Tathāgata wishes for people to know that the atoms, the world-systems, and the physical body are all equally illusory, false, and unreal. Although...
Since beauty and greatness have no connection whatsoever with true nature, he addressed Subhūti and questioned him, saying:
"What do you think? Suppose there were all the atoms contained within a great trichiliocosm."
Was that number ever truly great? As for the atoms of the world, how could they have any limit?
The Buddha merely took them as a metaphor to illustrate the vastness of human deluded thoughts.
Subhūti said, "Very many, World-Honored One. Subhūti answered with "very many" because the number of dust motes in a great trichiliocosm is immeasurable.
"Subhūti, as for those atoms, the Tathāgata says they are not atoms; they are called 'atoms.
Subhūti, having answered the Buddha’s question regarding the great number of atoms, the Buddha again addressed him by name, saying: 'As for these atoms...'"
The Buddha does not cling to the characteristics of even a single mote of dust. Since dust fundamentally has no connection with the self, it is said to be "not a mote of dust.
Nevertheless, the characteristic of dust remains distinct; thus, it is merely designated as a "mote of dust. This serves as a metaphor for deluded thoughts:
though they may be numerous, if one does not give rise to a mind that follows them, then deluded thoughts will likewise be unable to create an obstruction.
The Tathāgata speaks of the world as not being a world; it is merely named "the world.
Viewed from the perspective of the Buddha, not only are minute particles illusory and unreal, but even the vast world is likewise created by a single thought-moment of the human mind.
When consumed by the fires of the kalpa, it must ultimately perish. Therefore, it is said that although the Tathāgata speaks of the world, he does not cling to it.
The characteristics of the world are, in truth, not the world. Yet the world appears as it is; it is merely designated by the name "world.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks? The Buddha further said:

He addressed Subhūti, saying: "What do you think? As for the Tathāgata’s form-body, which possesses the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics—if one were to see these marks, could it be said that one truly sees the Tathāgata?

This was because he meant that although the Tathāgata’s form-body possesses various marks and characteristics, it too belongs to the realm of illusion and delusion; therefore, one should not rely on this to see him.
Thus it is with the Tathāgata. The *Raft Simile Sūtra* states: Regarding the thirty-two marks: first, the body is pure;
second, the body is upright and dignified, moving with the majesty of an elephant king; third, the body does not waver or lean; fourth, the deportment is complete;

fifth, the joints of the bones are like hooks and chains; sixth, extraordinary fragrances issue from the pores; seventh, a halo of light one fathom wide surrounds the body; eighth, the light shines forth...
9. He has a fleshly protuberance on the crown of his head (uṣṇīṣa). 10. His hair is long and beautiful. 11. His hair is deep blue-black and does not become disheveled.
12. His face is perfectly full like the full moon. 13. His eyebrows are like the crescent moon. 14.
Between his eyebrows is the mark of the white tuft of hair (ūrṇā-kośa). 15. His eyes are long and wide. 16. His nose is high and its nostrils do not show. 17. His ears...
