It is because such a person is treated with contempt and disdain by others in this present life that the transgressions and evils committed in their previous births are immediately eliminated and utterly destroyed within the realm of the unseen; moreover, it is not merely that they are extinguished.
Furthermore, one can attain the realization of the Dharma of unsurpassed enlightenment; how could the power of this sutra then be considered slight or insignificant?

Subhūti, I recall that in the past, during immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas before the time of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, I encountered eight hundred and forty thousand *koṭi-nayuta* Buddhas, all of whom I served and made offerings to, never letting my efforts go to waste.

"Zhe" (者) is pronounced "tuō" (拖) in the foreign [Sanskrit] sound. ○ *Asaṃkhyeya* (阿僧祇), in the language of the flowers [Chinese], means "immeasurable. *Nayuta* (那由他) means "ten million times ten million.
Furthermore, the Buddha cited his own merit from making offerings to Buddhas in the past to testify to the excellence of upholding this sutra;
therefore, he addressed Subhūti, saying: "I recall that in a past age, throughout immeasurable long kalpas, under my original teacher Dīpaṃkara..."
Prior to the time of the ancient Buddhas, I encountered countless Buddhas, all of whom I made offerings to and served;
there was never one who passed by me in vain without receiving my offerings and service. The merit resulting from this is indeed vast.

Furthermore, if there should be someone in the future final age who is able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the merit they obtain would not equal even one hundredth part of the merit from my own offerings to the Buddhas;
it would not equal one part in ten million, one billion, or even one trillion, nor could it be reached by any calculation or analogy.
To continue from the preceding point: although the merit of serving the Buddhas is great, yet...

If there should be someone in the world of the final age, when the faculty of faith has become increasingly thin and the path of the sutras is gradually extinguished, who is able to uphold and recite this sutra, then they may expect to realize awakening.

As for the merit thus obtained, compared to the merit of my own offerings to the Buddhas, even a hundred thousand million billionth part shall never equal even a single fraction of it. Thus it is said:
It reaches a level of merit beyond comparison, such that no other merit can even equal one part of it.
This is an extreme statement regarding the vastness of the merit from recitation; it cannot be matched by any other merit.

Subhūti, if a son or daughter of good family, in the final age at the end of time, should receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the merit they would thereby obtain—if I were to describe it in full, some who hear it might have their minds become deranged and, filled with doubt, fail to believe.
The Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying: "The merit of upholding this sutra that I have just mentioned was spoken only in brief."

It is merely this: if there are sons or daughters of good family who, during the time of the final age, are able to uphold and recite this sutra, the merit they shall obtain—if I were to describe it according to reality—some people might not understand the principles herein.
Upon suddenly hearing these words, their minds will surely be struck with alarm and delusion; they will instead become further confused and, filled with doubt, refuse to believe them.
This is what is meant by saying that [the truth] can be explained to those who understand it, but is difficult to discuss with worldly people.

As for those who doubt, the nature of the fox is to be suspicious; when crossing a river on ice during the winter, it walks upon the surface only fearing the ice might be thin and cause it to sink into the water. First, it goes...
By the riverbank, he listened for the sound of the water; after going back and forth several times, he finally crossed it—hence the term "hesitation" (*hu-yi*).
Subhūti, you should know that the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable, and its karmic fruition is likewise inconceivable.
The Buddha, having already spoken at length on the excellence of this sutra, again addressed Subhūti, saying: "You should know that the wondrous meaning of this sutra is inexhaustible;
it cannot be fathomed or recognized by those of shallow roots and inferior wisdom. Those who uphold and recite it will immediately obtain good fruits;
their meritorious retribution will be such that if they slander or disparage it, they will inevitably receive the karmic retribution of evil fruits. Such shall be their retribution.
All these matters are beyond the reach of mental calculation or deliberation; one must be cautious regarding them. Chapter Seventeen:
"Ultimately No-Self" states that the True Dharma of the Mahāyāna is ultimately characterized by non-attainment and non-exposition.
Furthermore, how could there be any marks of a self, a person, or the like within the True Dharma?

At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how should a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* abide? How should they subdue their minds?
At that moment, Subhūti [spoke] for the sake of those present in the assembly listening to the Dharma, as well as for future seekers of the Way, regarding what the Buddha was about to say.
Fearing that the method for dwelling the mind and subduing delusions may not yet be fully clear, he addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"Venerable One, if sons and daughters of good family give rise to the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, how should their true mind dwell?
And when deluded thoughts arise, how should they be subdued? This is the essential point of this entire sutra; therefore, I do not hesitate [to ask]."

This has been prolix; I shall once again set forth the questions and answers, desiring that all doubts be completely dispelled so that the path of cultivation may proceed without hindrance, thereby allowing the mind of universal salvation through compassion to be seen.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Good sons and good daughters who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should give rise to this thought:
'I should bring all sentient beings to final liberation (*parinirvāṇa*).
Since these are those who aspire to the Mahāyāna and must therefore give rise to the Great Mind, the Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying: 'Good sons and good daughters...'"
Those who have resolved to attain the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment should constantly give rise to such a thought: "I shall deliver and liberate all sentient beings.
This is the method for descending and abiding [in the world]. Indeed, those of the Two Vehicles seek only their own liberation, and thus their compassion is not universal.
Those whose aspiration seeks the Mahāyāna, though they themselves have not yet been liberated, must first seek to liberate others; this is the resolve of a Bodhisattva.
The mind [thinks]:
"Having brought all sentient beings to extinction (nirvāṇa), there is not a single sentient being who has actually been extinguished.
O sons and daughters of good family, although all sentient beings have already been delivered and liberated, the vow was not established in vain; yet, as for that mind—
He does not take credit for this himself, nor does he perceive even a single sentient being as having been brought to parinirvāṇa by him.
He gives rise to such a thought.
Why is this? Subhūti, if a bodhisattva possesses the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, or the notion of a life-span, [he cannot be called a bodhisattva].
Then they are not Bodhisattvas. As for those who deliver sentient beings without regarding sentient beings as "those delivered by me"—why is this so?

Subhūti, you should know that if a Bodhisattva maintains even a single thought of delivering sentient beings, they possess the four marks such as self and person, and are thus not a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva.
Why is this so, Subhūti? Truly, there is no dharma whatsoever that gives rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is it that a bodhisattva delivers sentient beings without grasping at signs?
Subhūti, you should know that in this unsurpassed true Dharma, there is truly no dharma of arising; yet one is able to give rise to unsurpassed awakening.
As for the mind: if one clings to signs while seeking the Way, it will ultimately be difficult to achieve success.
Subhūti, what do you think? Did the Tathāgata, at the time of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, obtain any dharma called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
The Buddha wished for people to have true faith that there is no mind that can be attained; therefore, he further cited [this example].
To test Subhūti’s own realization, he asked: "What do you think?
When I was formerly with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, did I ever possess any dharma by which I attained supreme enlightenment?"
"No, World-Honored One. As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no dharma by which the Buddha, under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti, through the Buddha’s question, realized that dharmas arise from self-awakening;
there is no dharma that can cause them to be so. Therefore, he answered with "No," and addressed the World-Honored One."

The Venerable One said: "As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, when I was with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, there was truly no dharma by which I could have attained this unsurpassed awakening; it was simply through my own realization."
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is, Subhūti! Truly, there is no dharma that the Tathāgata has attained as 'anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi'.
Because Subhūti’s response deeply accorded with his own intent, the Buddha approved of it and addressed him again, saying:
"In the past, at the place of my original teacher, although it was said that I had attained the Dharma, I also [attained]..."
There is nothing to be attained; it is not by means of some distinct dharma that one attains unsurpassed enlightenment.

Subhūti, if there were any dharma that the Tathāgata had attained as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, then Dīpaṃkara would not have granted me this prediction: "In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni."
“Nī” means “to bestow a prediction,” that is, to grant a prediction that one will attain the fruit in the future. “Śākya” is translated into Chinese as “Capable Benevolence” (Néngrén).
“Muni” is translated into Chinese as “Quiescence” (Jímèi). Quiescence is its essence, which is the character “Rú” (如);
capable benevolence is its function, which is the character “Lái” (來). The Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying: “If I had possessed any distinct dharma by which I could have attained [enlightenment],”
The Supreme Awakened One, my original teacher, did not bestow a prediction upon me, yet he said: "In a future life, you shall attain Buddhahood, and your name shall be Śākyamuni.
It appears that regarding those who receive such a prediction, within the act of bestowing and receiving it, there is neither attainment nor non-attainment;
it is not a matter of some secret transmission. If there were even a hair’s breadth of deliberate action involved, it would certainly not be the Great [Way].
I have mounted upon the True Dharma.

Because there is truly no dharma by which one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, therefore the Buddha Dīpaṃkara conferred upon me this prediction, saying: "In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni."
Because it was precisely through the fact that I possess no distinct dharma that I achieved unsurpassed enlightenment,
my Original Teacher bestowed upon me a prophecy, saying: "In a future age, you shall certainly attain Buddhahood, and your name shall be Śākyamuni."
Why is this? The Tathāgata is the very meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena. Why was our former teacher given the Buddha-name Śākyamuni?
It is because the four characters "Śākyamuni" also proclaim the meaning of the Tathāgata;
and the Tathāgata is the spontaneous nature of the suchness of all phenomena. How can people fail to consider the significance of the name?
And contemplate its meaning!
If someone were to say, "The Tathāgata has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*," Subhūti, there is truly no dharma by which the Buddha has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. If one speaks of me...
Having received the teacher’s prediction, all claimed to have attained the Dharma. Because of this, I said:
"Subhūti, you should know that as for my attainment of the Dharma of Unsurpassed Enlightenment, it is nothing more than the clarity of one's own mind;
there is merely the name 'attainment of the Dharma,' but in reality, there is no trace of attaining the Dharma. For this reason, it is called the attainment of Unsurpassed Enlightenment."
Subhūti, the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* attained by the Tathāgata is, within it, neither substantial nor void.

Subhūti, you should know that when I speak of attaining the dharma of unsurpassed enlightenment, if one were to ask about this, it is not a case of there being a substantial trace such that there is truly something attained;
nor is it a false statement such that there is absolutely nothing attained. This is because...
The Middle Way is known only by the wise. To speak of existence or non-existence is, in every case, mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Therefore, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma. Subhūti, what is called "all dharmas" is not actually all dharmas;
it is for this reason that they are called "all dharmas. For this reason, the Tathāgata [teaches] for your sake...
All the teachings on the Dharma that have been spoken, though they lack a fixed direction, are all established in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings to lead them toward the profound.

Thus, whatever has been spoken is nothing other than the Buddha-dharma. Subhūti, you should know that in my instruction of others, all the various dharmas spoken do not exceed guiding them according to their respective faculties; though there is but a single voice, it is manifested in diverse ways.

While the understandings derived from hearing differ, they are in truth not of two natures. This is unlike all the teachings of ordinary people and externalists, which each have their own distinct differences.
It is merely through skillful means that various analogies are expounded; for this reason, it is called "all dharmas."
"Subhūti, it is as if there were a person whose body was vast and tall. This is the Tathāgata further demonstrating the meaning of being free from marks;
therefore, he calls out to Subhūti and interrogates him, saying: "Suppose what I have described as a human body were as large as Mount Sumeru."
“Is his body large and tall?
Subhūti replied, “World-Honored One, when the Tathāgata speaks of a person’s body being large and tall, it is not a large body;
it is called a ‘large body’ [only figuratively]. Subhūti, understanding the Buddha’s intention, addressed the World-Honored One, saying, “I, the Tathāgata...”
That which is described as the "great body of a human being" refers to the magnitude of the form-body (*rūpakāya*). Ultimately, it belongs to the realm of illusion and unreality;
it is not like the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which exists eternally and is indestructible. Therefore, although it is great, it is not a "great body.
Nevertheless, because its physical characteristics (*rūpalakṣaṇa*) remain manifest, it is designated by the name "great body."
Subhūti, it is the same for a bodhisattva. If one were to say, "I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa," then that person would not be called a bodhisattva.

The Buddha, because the meaning of Subhūti’s statement regarding the "great body" deeply accords with his own intent, addressed Subhūti and said: "Although a person who is a bodhisattva sets their will upon saving sentient beings..."
Furthermore, one should regard it as being like the illusory nature of a "great body," and thus not maintain the view that there are beings to be delivered.
If one were to say, "I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to extinction," then that mind would perceive that there are beings to be delivered.
This would constitute grasping at signs; such a person could not be called a bodhisattva.

Why is this? Subhūti, in reality there is no dharma that can be called "bodhisattva. As for why one who practices the deliverance of sentient beings while clinging to signs is not called a bodhisattva: Subhūti, you should know that although a person who is a bodhisattva possesses...
To practice and realize [the truth] without grasping at the characteristics of phenomena—this is what is called a bodhisattva.
For this reason, the Buddha taught that all dharmas are without self, without a person, without a sentient being, and without a life-span.
Therefore, I have always told you: one should eliminate attachment to all Buddha-dharmas and not maintain the notions of "person" or "self."
Only with such views can there be the True Dharma.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to say, "I shall adorn the Buddha-fields," he cannot be called a bodhisattva.
Now, when a bodhisattva delivers sentient beings, they should not cling to signs; likewise, they should not become attached to signs even regarding the adornment [of the Buddha-field].
Subhūti, you should know that if a bodhisattva says, "I shall adorn the Buddha-field," then such a person cannot truly be called a bodhisattva.
For the one who adorns the pure land does so by purifying their own mind. Not...
To give rise to the perception of grasping is what constitutes the adornment of one's own Buddha-land.
If one is attached to the intention of adornment—such as constructing stupas and temples with various decorations—it cannot be called true adornment at all.
Why is this? When the Tathāgata speaks of adorning buddha-fields, it is not actually adorning; it is merely called "adorning.
Why is it that what is called "adornment through attachment to signs" is not so? It is because that which I have spoken of as adorning buddha-fields—
To have only the name of adornment while no trace of adornment remains— this is precisely what is called "adornment.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva penetrates the dharma of non-self, the Tathāgata says that such a person is truly a bodhisattva.
Subhūti, you should know that saving sentient beings constitutes benefiting others, while adornment constitutes benefiting oneself.
A bodhisattva, being able to benefit both self and others, does not grasp at signs. However, there is no greater affliction than having a body.
The sentient beings of the world all harbor the view of self within their minds; consequently, they give rise to various deluded attachments from which they cannot escape.

This is due to the burden of clinging to a self. If a bodhisattva can dispel attachment to the grasping at a self and realize that the person and the self are one and the same, such a person has attained penetration into the dharma of non-self. I declare that this person may be called a true bodhisattva.
Indeed! Those who seek the Way must first exhaust all human desires; only then will the Heavenly Principle flow forth.
If there is even the slightest obstruction, it will be difficult to expect enlightenment. Those with hearts set upon this Way must first be free from the self.
Chapter Eighteen: The Section on the Single Essence and Unified Contemplation.

It is said that the Tathāgata’s great compassion contemplates all beings with equality, harboring no thoughts of self-interest and forming no views of disparaging others. Being supremely impartial and free from partiality, he has attained realization that exhausts the entire dharma-realm.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye?
That which the Tathāgata has realized—the five eyes and six supernormal powers—is far beyond the reach of his peers; even Bodhisattvas cannot fathom its ultimate limit.
Yet the reason for this is simply that, with a mind of equanimity, he practices the conduct of universal salvation. Thus, [the Buddha] addressed Subhūti.
He questioned him, saying: "What do you think? Does the Tathāgata’s form-body possess a fleshly eye? Subhūti replied:
"Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses a fleshly eye. Subhūti [spoke thus] because the Tathāgata’s form-body was present.
Therefore, they are identical. Yet it is said that the Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*).
Although the Tathāgata’s fleshly eye appears no different from that of ordinary people, in reality it is not different, yet it is different.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye? "It is so, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata possesses the divine eye. The Buddha asked Subhūti again, saying, "Does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye?
Because Subhūti was endowed with the five eyes of a Buddha, he answered that the Tathāgata possessed the divine eye.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the wisdom-eye (prajñā-cakṣus)? "He replied, 'So it is, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata possesses the wisdom-eye. Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the dharma-eye (dharma-cakṣus)? "He replied, 'So it is, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata possesses the dharma-eye. Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the buddha-eye (buddha-cakṣus)? "He replied, 'So it is.'"
"World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye. Subhūti answered all the questions regarding the various eyes without any variation in his words;
this was merely from the perspective of what he could perceive. However, as for the objects perceived by the Buddha’s five eyes, these are beyond the capacity of Subhūti to know.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "As for the five eyes: with the flesh eye, one sees all forms; with the divine eye, one sees..."
The mind of all sentient beings is perceived by the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), which perceives the faculties and spheres of sentient beings;

the dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*) perceives the characteristics of all phenomena and their true reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*); and the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*) perceives the ten powers (*daśabala*) of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, an ancient master’s verse states:

"The divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) is unobstructed, while the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) is obstructed and lacks penetration. The wisdom-eye contemplates only the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), while the dharma-eye thoroughly knows emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The Buddha-eye..."
Like a thousand suns, though they illuminate different bodies, they are ultimately the same. These five eyes pervade all ten realms, yet they differ in their degrees of excellence;
if they belong to a Tathāgata, they are all simply the Buddha-eye.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Regarding all the sands in the Ganges River, does the Buddha say they are sand?

"So it is, World-Honored One; the Tathāgata says they are sand. The Buddha, wishing to provide a metaphor for the abundance of the deluded minds of sentient beings, first interrogated Subhūti regarding the sands in the Ganges, saying: "Regarding all the sands in the Ganges River, the Buddha also..."
"Is this sand or not? Subhūti perceived no difference between it and sand; therefore, he accepted it as such and said, "The Tathāgata says this is sand. Subhūti, what do you think?
If there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in a single Ganges River, and if there were as many [worlds] as there are grains of sand in all those rivers...
The Ganges. As many as are the grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers, so many are the Buddha-worlds. Are they not indeed many?
This Buddha uses the world as a metaphor for the abundance of the deluded mind; therefore, he calls out to Subhūti and interrogates him, saying:
"In your view, suppose the number of grains of sand in a single Ganges River were such that each grain of sand became a [Buddha-world]..."
“Ganges. Suppose there were as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers—would that also be considered much?

“Very much, World-Honored One. Subhūti [thought]: “If even a single world-system equal in size to the sands of the Ganges is already immeasurably much, how much more so would it be for Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of all those Ganges Rivers! Thus, he answered, “Very much.”
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "In all those lands, the Tathāgata fully knows the various kinds of minds of all sentient beings.
Because Subhūti had already replied that the worlds were exceedingly numerous, the Buddha further addressed him, saying:
"You know that the Buddha-worlds are as numerous as the sands of many Ganges Rivers; yet do you also know those lands?"
The deluded minds of sentient beings within this world—are they not even more numerous?
Now, if the deluded mind of a single person is already such as this, then the deluded minds of all people are infinite and utterly beyond calculation.
Yet, although they possess various kinds of minds, when I observe them with my Buddha-eye, I know and see them all. For though the multitude of minds is vast, they are none other than [the one mind].
It is merely a fabrication.
Why? Because the Tathāgata says that all minds are "not-minds," yet they are called "minds.
As for what is meant by saying, "I am able to fully know the various minds of sentient beings," it is because I say that those various minds are nothing other than [the absence of self].
Delusion is entirely incapable of being the mind of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Nevertheless, both truth and delusion arise from the one mind;
thus, they are also designated as "mind. Why is this so?
Subhūti, the past mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended; the future [mind]...
The coming mind cannot be apprehended. Now, what is it that I mean by "the many minds are not the mind"?
Subhūti, you should know that although truth and falsehood differ, they do not, in total, transcend the three measures of mind:
past, present, and future. For the past mind has already passed away and perished; the present mind shifts and passes away from moment to moment; and the future mind is as yet unarisen.

It has not yet arrived; from where, then, could one seek the mind? Alas, sentient beings do not understand this principle and instead pursue deluded thoughts, undergoing illusory transformations and wandering through the cycle of existence. For this reason, mental thoughts are so numerous that they have no end;
such is the nature of arising and ceasing. If one allows thoughts to arise but does not follow after them, then there will be thought without thinking, and thinking without thought. Even if...
There are three minds and ten thousand thoughts, yet none can act as an obstruction.
Reflect upon this. ○ Chapter Nineteen: The Universal Transformation of the Dharma Realm. It is said that the Buddha-mind is impartial;
throughout the entire Dharma realm, there is nowhere it does not flow and transform. If one takes the merit of bestowing jewels and enters the mind of formlessness, then the three...
The essence of the wheel is emptiness; this is why the Dharma-realm is able to transform all beings universally.

Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would that person, by reason of this, acquire much merit? Herein, the Buddha again raises the subject of the gift of jewels.
The merit obtained vanishes in the blink of an eye and becomes empty; moreover, it has no connection whatsoever with the nature of the mind.
Desiring to urge people toward the path of cultivation, he called out to Subhūti and questioned him, saying: "What do you think?
If someone were to fill a great trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would that person, by virtue of the causal conditions of giving those treasures, [attain great merit]?"
"Would the merit he thereby obtains not be great?
"It would be so, Blessed One; by this cause and condition, this person would obtain very great merit.
Subhūti, if one were to calculate it by way of worldly rewards, the merit obtained by this person through the gift of jewels would indeed be immeasurable.
It is immeasurable. Therefore, he answers with "very much.
Subhūti, if merit were substantial, the Tathāgata would not say that one obtains much merit.
Although the Buddha obtains great merit through the gift of jewels, it has no relation whatsoever to the nature of the mind; thus, he addresses Subhūti, saying: "This..."

The merit of giving material wealth ultimately results in something illusory and vain. If one truly provides relief within the nature of the mind, the Tathāgata would not say that such a person has acquired much merit.
This is because the merit of giving material wealth merely yields worldly rewards.
Practitioners do not take [this as their goal], because it lacks true merit.

Although the Tathāgata says that one gains much merit, this is because the merit derived from the gift of jewels provides no actual benefit to the work of the mind-ground; therefore, the Tathāgata merely says that one gains much merit.
However, although the retribution of merit may be vast, it ultimately comes to an end; thus, what is there to say for such trivial enjoyment?
The Buddha’s intent was surely to urge the diligent cultivation of supramundane merit, rather than merely planting mundane blessings and virtues.
Chapter Twenty: Detaching from Form and Detaching from Characteristics. It is said that when a person wishes to see the Buddha, they must seek him by detaching from form and characteristics.
Only when one sees the Tathāgata of Self-Nature can it be called true seeing; one should not seek the True Buddha within form and characteristics.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Buddha be seen by means of a body endowed with physical form?

The Buddha feared that people would be deluded regarding their own minds as being the Buddha—given that the words "one's own mind is the Buddha"—and instead seek the Buddha within external physical characteristics.
Therefore, he called out to Subhūti and questioned him, saying: "What do you think?
If a person wishes to see the Buddha, may they see him merely by means of the colors of the various marks upon his feet?"
"No, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata should not be seen by means of the body of form.

Having heard these words of the Buddha's inquiry, Subhūti understood that one seeks the Buddha through the body of form, but that this is not the Dharma-body, the true Buddha; therefore, he answered with "No."

To say that one wishes to see the Tathāgata, one should not seek to see him merely by means of his perfected physical body (*rūpakāya*). Why is this? "To say that all dharmas are annihilated—do not conceive such a thought. The Buddha then addressed Subhūti, saying:
"If you were to conceive such a thought, then those who have set their minds upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment would likewise speak of all dharmas as being annihilated."
"All have been completely extinguished. You must be careful not to harbor such a thought; I urge you again and again. Why is this?
Those who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* do not speak of the characteristic of extinction regarding phenomena.
This is why I instruct you not to form this notion. Why would one fall into the view of annihilationism? It is because... [the resolve] has arisen.
Regarding this mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, it is certainly never said that there is a characteristic of cessation within the true dharma of bodhi.
If a dharma were subject to cessation, how could it be called the unsurpassed true dharma?

Chapter Twenty-Eight: Non-acceptance and Non-attachment. It is said that although a bodhisattva cultivates all manner of wholesome deeds, they harbor no intention of seeking to receive merit for themselves;
it is precisely because of this non-attachment that their merit becomes increasingly superior.
“Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to take seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and offer them as a gift, the Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying:
‘If there were a bodhisattva who took the seven treasures of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and offered them as a gift, the merit they would obtain would indeed be great.
Yet, this is still surpassed by the merit of seeking the Way through the signless (animitta).’”
It is incomparable.
Furthermore, if there is another person who knows that all phenomena are without self and attains patience (*kṣānti*), this bodhisattva surpasses the merit obtained by the former bodhisattva.
If there is yet another bodhisattva who knows that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions...
Birth is without intrinsic nature. Because it is without intrinsic nature, there is no self. When there is no self, all marks are entirely free from attachment.

Cultivating in this manner, one will surely attain perfect enlightenment. To investigate the reason why this is achieved, the point where power is gained lies entirely in applying oneself to the single character "patience" (kṣānti).
For when there is no contention with anything, greed and selfishness are easily removed; once selfishness is gone, [the mind becomes tranquil].
Illumination. Through illumination, awakening arises and one reaches the Way. This is the merit of realizing the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) cultivated by this bodhisattva;
is it not far superior to the merit obtained by the former bodhisattva through the gift of jewels?
This passage instructs people not to covet tainted karmic rewards (*sāsrava-vipāka*), but rather to cultivate the merit of realizing the nature of reality.
Why is this? Subhūti, it is because bodhisattvas do not accept merit. What is meant by "the merit of cultivation through nature" surpassing that of the gift of superior jewels?
Subhūti, you should know that because of the practice maintained by these bodhisattvas, they never have a mind that greedily accepts merit; therefore, they surpass those [who give jewels].
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, why is it that a bodhisattva does not accept merit?
Having heard the Buddha’s words regarding not accepting merit, Subhūti immediately suspected that this meant a refusal to accept it;
therefore, he addressed the Buddha, referring to him as World-Honored One, and asked: "In the cultivation of a bodhisattva, for what reason is merit not accepted?"
"Subhūti, a bodhisattva should not be greedily attached to the merit they have performed; therefore, it is said that they do not 'receive' merit.
Because Subhūti had misunderstood the meaning of "not receiving merit," the Buddha called to him and addressed him, saying:
The merit produced by a bodhisattva is not necessarily rejected and not accepted; rather, one should simply not give rise to a mind of greedy attachment.
For this reason, it is said that "merit is not received. However, by merely not giving rise to greedy attachment, the merit one receives becomes even greater.
Chapter Twenty-nine: On the Tranquility of Dignified Conduct. It is said that the Buddha’s Dharmakāya is pure, quiescent, and unconditioned;
it possesses no characteristics of coming or going, sitting or reclining. One should not seek the Tathāgata within these [physical manifestations].
Subhūti, if anyone were to say that the Tathāgata comes or goes, sits or lies down, such a person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught.
This is the Buddha’s repeated statement that the Dharma-body is not a mark, and he concludes with this.
Therefore, he addresses Subhūti, saying: "If someone says that the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of physical marks, why now..."
Whether coming, going, sitting, or reclining—amidst these four modes of deportment—one beholds the physical marks of the Buddha’s body, yet it is not that the Tathāgata himself is present therein.

However, this is merely the Buddha of the specific physical marks (lakṣaṇa-kāya-buddha) and not the Buddha of the Dharma-body (dharma-kāya-buddha). To behold only these marks while failing to seek the realization of one's nature is [inadequate].
What benefit is there for oneself? I say that such a person will ultimately not understand the meaning of "signlessness" (animitta) as previously explained by me.
Why is this? One who comes from nowhere and goes nowhere is therefore called a Tathāgata. Thus it is said.
What does it mean that this person does not understand the meaning of what I have said? It is because the Tathāgata is truly without the characteristics of coming or going;

he abides in suchness (tathatā), and is therefore called the Tathāgata. Why do you not contemplate the name to seek its meaning and thereby attain right view, yet instead wish to seek him within physical forms? How could that be possible?
Section Thirty: On the Single Unified Characteristic. It is said that the world is vast;

yet it is also composed of the aggregation of myriad particles, forming something illusory, delusive, and unreal. Therefore, it is said that the mundane world is what ordinary people fail to understand, taking it to be real and true.
This is merely because they do not know the meaning of the "single unified characteristic."
“Subhūti, if a son or daughter of good family were to grind this trichiliocosm into fine dust, what do you think?
Would that mass of dust be great? The Buddha spoke thus because he considered the atoms of the world to be entirely illusory and unreal;
fearing that people might take the world and its dust to be truly real, he addressed Subhūti.
Lifting it up, he questioned him, saying: "In this present world, everything is formed through the aggregation of various particles.
Suppose there were virtuous men and women who were to break down a trichiliocosm into minute particles. What do you think—would the number of these particles be considered many?
When he replied that, if one seeks by grasping at characteristics, the particles would be infinitely numerous, [the Master said]: "Indeed..."
The metaphor of motes of dust illustrates the abundance of deluded thoughts. If a person gives rise to a mind that clings to delusion, then deluded thoughts will become even more numerous.
If one allows suffering to arise and cease as it may, yet the mind does not follow after it, then although deluded thoughts are many, they cannot cause one harm.
Subhūti said, "Very many, World-Honored One. Subhūti understood the Buddha’s intention in asking;
he knew that if one were to calculate by means of the minute particles of the world-systems, they would not be surpassed in their multitude. Therefore, he answered with the words "very many."
Why is this? If these multitudes of atoms were truly existent, the Buddha would not have called them "multitudes of atoms.
What does it mean for the dust to be "much"? It is because these many atoms are illusory and false, subject to arising and ceasing, and impermanent.
If one were to calculate their true existence based on the multiplicity of these atoms, the Buddha would not say that they constitute a "multitude of atoms."
Although the multitude of atoms is vast, it has no connection with me.
Why is this? The Buddha taught that the multitude of atoms is not a multitude of atoms; it is merely designated as a "multitude of atoms."

What is meant by saying that "dust" is not substantially existent? It is because when the Buddha speaks of the multiplicity of subtle particles (*paramāṇu*), he does not intend to establish the characteristic of a multiplicity of subtle particles as being real.
Rather, while the appearance of dust remains distinct, it is merely designated as "a multiplicity of subtle particles."
“World-Honored One, that which the Tathāgata has spoken of as a trichiliocosm is not a world; it is merely named a ‘world.

Subhūti, because he was discussing the illusory unreality of atoms and further inferred that the world itself is not real, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying: ‘That which is illusory and unreal is not limited to the smallness of atoms alone.’”
It is so. Even the vastness of the world is composed of accumulated dust; it cannot be regarded as truly real or indestructible.
That the world currently appears intact is merely what we conventionally call "the world.
For it is only the true nature that remains constant throughout all kalpas; all other material things must eventually perish. Therefore—
"It is not real," he said. "It is simply that people of the world do not know this; they all generally mistake illusions for reality, thereby forming inverted views.
Why is this? If the world were truly existent, it would be a 'unified whole' (*ekapiṇḍa*). The Tathāgata speaks of a 'unified whole' [only as a conventional designation]."
Thus, it is not a unified whole; yet it is called a unified whole. Why is it said that so-called worlds are not real?
If one were to regard a world as truly existent, one would fail to realize that it is composed of the aggregation of many particles;
it would then be merely a single phenomenon of combination. Therefore, when the Tathāgata speaks of this unified whole, he does not maintain the existence of even a single [independent] unity.
Regarding the view of a "combined aggregate" (*saṃghāta-lakṣaṇa*): as long as such a characteristic exists, it is merely termed a "combined aggregate.
Subhūti, that which is a combined aggregate is ineffable; yet ordinary people greedily cling to it.
Because the Buddha recognized that Subhūti’s response had profoundly grasped the essence of signlessness (*animitta*), he called out to him again and said:
He said: "That which is called the 'single unified mark' (ekapiṇḍalakṣaṇa) should not only not be viewed as real; it cannot even admit of verbal expression.
Yet, ordinary people of the world do not understand this principle, and consequently regard the realm of dust and phenomena as truly existent."
Yet the mind gives rise to grasping and attachment, thereby causing various afflictions to arise in confusion,
much like dust and mist obscuring the sky and depriving it of its clarity. However, once the mind does not cling to objects, then objects will no longer obstruct the person,
and the pure light will emerge once more.
Section Thirty-one: On the Non-arising of Knowledge and Views. It is said that practitioners of the Way should purify and eliminate all knowledge and views;
even regarding the True Dharma, they should not give rise to a mind of attachment or grasping. This is what is meant by the non-arising of knowledge and views.

"Subhūti, if someone were to say: 'The Buddha has spoken of the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span,' Subhūti, what do you think? Would such a person have understood the meaning of what I have taught?

This is the Buddha’s explicit statement regarding the teaching on the transcendence of marks (*lakṣaṇa*), serving as the conclusion of the sutra. For while marks are coarse, views are subtle; thus they are termed "views. The Buddha addressed Subhūti...
Bodhi said: "If someone were to say, 'The Buddha has preached the Dharma for you, yet he constantly refers to me as having a life-span,' this is the view of the four [extremes].
One should simply abandon or adopt these four views. Such a person likely does not yet understand;
Subhūti, what do you think? Would that person truly be able to comprehend the meaning of the four views I have explained?"
"No. This is because [the Buddha] wished to verify it through Subhūti’s reply.
'No, World-Honored One; this person does not understand the meaning of what the Tathāgata has spoken.
Subhūti, knowing the intent of the Buddha's question, answered with 'No,' and further addressed the World-Honored One, saying: 'I recognize this person; indeed...'"
They do not understand the meaning of the four views taught by the Tathāgata.
Why is this? When the World-Honored One speaks of the view of self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span, these are not actually views of a self.
The view of a person (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*), the view of a sentient being (*sattva-dṛṣṭi*), and the view of a life-span (*jīva-dṛṣṭi*)—these are called the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
As for what is meant by "the person does not understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught":
it is because the Lord has stated that these views of self, person, and life-span are to be abandoned and not to be clung to; this is what is meant.
“Subhūti, this is merely my view regarding the lifespan of human life.

Subhūti, those who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should know all phenomena in this way, see them in this way, and resolve with faith in this way, so that they do not give rise to the notion of a phenomenon (*dharma-saṃjñā*). Thus spoke the Buddha to Subhūti.

His answer perfectly accorded with the intent of the question. Therefore, he addressed him again, saying: "Regarding what is called 'seeing' and 'non-seeing,' not only should the four views be abandoned;

even for one who has resolved to attain supreme enlightenment, although they speak of seeking the Way, regarding all true dharmas, they should simply know them thus, see them thus, and believe and understand them thus."
Awakening means not giving rise to discrimination therein, nor giving rise to a mind that clings to dharmas so as to form the marks of dharmas.
Such is the understanding seen previously.
Subhūti, as for what is called the "marks of dharmas," the Tathāgata says they are not marks of dharmas; they are merely named "marks of dharmas."

Subhūti, you should know this: that which is called the characteristic of dharmas (dharmalakṣaṇa) should not be grasped. To grasp at the characteristic of arising is not the characteristic of dharmas;
if one gives rise to grasping, this is what is called the characteristic of dharmas.

○ Section on the Non-Reality of Manifested Transformations (in thirty-two words): Regarding the appearance of a Buddha in the world, he comes specifically to transform and deliver sentient beings through his manifestations.
Yet, within this dream-like and illusory human existence, he especially teaches the cultivation of the "illusion-like" Dharma-gate, so that one does not mistake it for something truly real.

Subhūti, if someone were to take seven treasures filling immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds and offer them as a gift, the merit of that gift of treasures described in the sūtras would not equal the merit of upholding and explaining these words. This has been stated repeatedly;

yet, because the Buddha ultimately feared that people might greedily seek after the reward of merit while disregarding the practice of cultivation, he specifically repeats this here to conclude the whole.
The intent of this sutra is profound. The Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying:
"Suppose there were someone who, with the seven treasures filling immeasurable and innumerable worlds, were to offer them as a gift.
The magnitude of such a gift would far surpass that of the great trichiliocosm, and the merit thereby obtained would likewise be exceedingly vast. Yet, compared to the gift of the Dharma..."
Although such merit is great, it ultimately has its limit.

If there are good sons or good daughters who give rise to the bodhicitta and uphold this sutra—even as little as a single four-line verse—receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, and explaining it for others, their merit shall surpass that of the aforementioned gift of jewels. "That" refers to the gift of jewels.

The merit is indeed great. If there are sons or daughters of good family who give rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment and uphold this sutra—even if they maintain only a single four-line verse—and having practiced it themselves, further expound its meaning to others, then their merit far surpasses that of the one who gives the gift of jewels. As for the exposition...
The explanation is even more subtle.
How does one expound it for others? One does not grasp at appearances; one remains as suchness, unmoving.

Thus, when expounding the meaning of the sutras for others, what should the result be like? One must simply remain unattached to everything and not involve oneself with names or appearances. And so forth.
The true nature is perfectly luminous; it is eternally as-it-is, profoundly still and unmoving, devoid of the characteristics of coming and going, birth and extinction.
To speak in this manner is to be skilled in exposition, so that those who hear may all obtain benefit.
Why is this? All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows; they are like dew and like lightning—one should contemplate them in this way.

As for what is called "preaching the Dharma without grasping at signs," why is that? It is because engaging with names and signs is a worldly phenomenon (*laukika-dharma*), not a supramundane phenomenon (*lokottara-dharma*).
The world consists of conditioned phenomena, and these conditioned phenomena are merely provisional.
They are not real. They are like the emptiness of dream-objects; like the delusion of magical transformations; like bubbles on water, arising and ceasing in an instant;
like reflections in a mirror, suddenly appearing and suddenly vanishing; like morning dew, easily dried away; and like flashes of lightning, abruptly extinguished.
To contemplate these conditioned phenomena through these six analogies is what constitutes right contemplation. If...
Any other contemplation is called false contemplation; let students examine this with care.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Elder Subhūti, along with the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, [and upāsikās], [rejoiced and practiced accordingly].
O Upāsikā, when all the world—including devas, humans, and asuras—heard what the Buddha had spoken, they were all greatly rejoiced;

they believed, accepted, and practiced it. When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, at that time the Elder Subhūti who was present in the assembly, as well as the ordained monks and nuns, the laymen who were upāsakas, and the women who were upāsikās...
The *yī* [non-humans], as well as all the devas, humans, and asuras of the world, upon hearing this sutra preached, all attained realization and were filled with great joy;
they received it with devout faith and respectfully practiced its teachings.
Now that those who heard the sutra at that time have each departed having obtained their benefit, my wish is that until the end of the future, whether they hear it or...
May we see [the Buddha] together and realize Bodhi; this is my profound aspiration.
*The Easy Explanation of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Vol. II (End).
